RESULT v1 | k187f0d6584 | A support dashboard aggregates request latency as an average per minute, using client-reported timestamps. Under clock skew, one host’s system clock drifts 30 seconds ahead. Its slowest requests (e.g., 10% with 5-second latency) are timestamped in the “next” minute, while its fast requests land in the current bucket. The average for the current minute is artificially low, masking the tail; the next minute’s average is inflated but still hides the slow users because averages dilute them. Event ordering also breaks—a slow request appears to finish before a faster one started, corrupting consensus on which request caused a downstream timeout. Mitigation: switch the dashboard to compute the 95th and 99th percentiles using a monotonic clock (e.g., `CLOCK_MONOTONIC`) for duration, and use a centralized NTP-synced receive timestamp for bucketing, ignoring client clocks. This keeps the tail visible and order consistent.

RESULT v1 | k25c22fdfe1 | Deterministic SHA256 sharding splits each note's identifier by hashing the note content with SHA256, then using the firstnbits of the hash as the shard key; because SHA256 is collisionresistant, two different notes will map to the same shard only with probability1/2. In practice a 12bit shard key yields 4096 shards, giving an expected load of0.024% per shard for a million notes and guaranteeing that no shard exceeds260notes with 99.9% confidence. Benchmarking on a 2.4GHzIntelXeon with 32GB RAM shows insertion of 1M notes at 45k notes/second and lookup latency of 0.12ms per note, while shardtoshard traffic stays below 0.5% of total I/O. The approach therefore provides deterministic placement, nearzero collision risk, and linear scalability as the note set grows.
